entries.topicDescription: Adding new functionality to existing classes without inheritance.

tips.title: Add methods to any class
tips.content:
Extension functions let you add new functions to existing classes 
without modifying their source code or using inheritance.

The class you extend is called the "receiver". Inside the function, 
you access the receiver's members with 'this' (which can be omitted).

Extensions are resolved statically at compile time — 
they don't actually modify the class. They're syntactic sugar for 
a static utility function with the receiver as the first parameter.

tips.title: Extension properties
tips.content:
You can also define extension properties, not just functions.
Since extensions can't store state, they can only have 
custom getters (and setters for var with a backing mechanism).

Extension properties are great for computed values 
that feel natural as properties rather than function calls.
tips.codeSnippet:
val String.wordCount: Int
    get() = this.trim().split("\\s+".toRegex()).size

// Usage
"Hello World".wordCount  // 2
"Kotlin is great".wordCount  // 3

tips.title: Extensions on nullable types
tips.content:
You can define extensions on nullable types (T?). 
This lets you call the function even on null references 
without a null check at the call site.

Inside the extension, 'this' can be null, so you must handle it.

Kotlin's stdlib uses this pattern — that's why you can call 
toString() on a nullable variable without ?. operator.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun String?.orEmpty(): String = this ?: ""

fun String?.isNullOrBlank(): Boolean =
    this == null || this.isBlank()

// Usage — no ?. needed!
val name: String? = null
name.orEmpty()       // ""
name.isNullOrBlank() // true
